AI Science Explainer

A curious, patient explainer for anything from black holes to how vaccines are tested. It starts simple, uses everyday examples and goes deeper only when you ask.

TL;DR
  • Best for understanding concepts, news headlines and homework topics.
  • Tell it your level and ask for an everyday analogy first.
  • Ask for sources and double-check important facts.

What this coach helps with

  • Understanding a science topic from zero
  • Making sense of a health or science headline
  • Helping kids with curious questions
  • Preparing for an exam
  • Comparing what is known and what is still debated

Prompts you can copy

Copy a prompt, paste it into the Zehn AI Chat or any AI assistant, and replace the parts in [brackets] with your own details.

  1. Explain [topic] as if I'm 12, then again as if I'm a university student.

  2. I read this headline: [headline]. What does the research probably say, and what questions should I ask before believing it?

  3. Give me an everyday analogy for [concept], then tell me where the analogy breaks down.

  4. My child asked me [question]. Help me answer in three simple sentences and suggest a home experiment.

  5. Quiz me on [topic] with five questions, from easy to hard, and explain any I get wrong.

  6. What do scientists agree on about [topic], and what is still debated?

  7. Explain the difference between [concept A] and [concept B] with a table.

  8. Walk me through how [process, e.g. photosynthesis] works step by step, one step per message.

  9. Make me a one-page cheat sheet on [topic] for an exam, with the 10 key facts.

  10. What are three common myths about [topic], and what is the evidence against each?

  11. Explain how scientists know [fact, e.g. the age of the universe]. What is the evidence?

  12. Recommend how I could learn [field] from zero in 30 days, 20 minutes a day.

Two example conversations

Written by the Intellect AI team to show the style of answers. Not a real user conversation.

ExampleWhy is the sky blue?

YouMy daughter asked why the sky is blue and I didn't know.

Science ExplainerSunlight looks white but is a mix of all colours. When it hits the air, the tiny gas molecules scatter short blue light in every direction much more than red light. So blue reaches your eyes from all over the sky. At sunset light travels through more air, so the blue gets scattered away and reds remain.

ExampleReading a health headline

YouA headline says coffee adds years to your life. Is that true?

Science ExplainerUsually such headlines come from observational studies: coffee drinkers lived longer on average, but that doesn't prove coffee caused it. They may also sleep, eat or earn differently. Good questions: how many people, was it a trial or an observation, and who funded it? Your own doctor is the right person for personal advice.

Tips for better answers

  • Say what you already know; it saves you from explanations that are too easy or too hard.
  • Ask “How do we know?”. Evidence is the most interesting part of science.
  • For health topics, use the explainer to understand, and your doctor to decide.
  • AI can be confidently wrong; check key facts with a textbook or trusted source.

Questions people ask

Can I trust AI explanations of science?

For well-established basics, AI explanations are usually good. They can still contain mistakes, especially with numbers, recent research and niche topics. Ask for the reasoning and sources, compare with a trusted textbook or official website, and be most careful with health topics. Treat the AI as a starting point.

Is the science explainer good for homework?

Yes, as a tutor rather than a shortcut. Ask it to explain a concept, give an analogy, quiz you and check your reasoning. Write the answers yourself, because that is how you remember them, and follow your school's rules on using AI. A cheat sheet made together can help revision.

How do I get a simpler explanation?

Ask for a specific level, like “explain it to a 12-year-old”, and request an everyday analogy. If it still feels hard, ask it to explain only the first step, or to define every term it uses. You can always ask for the more detailed version afterwards.

Can the science explainer give medical advice?

No. It can explain how the body works, what a study design means or what a term on a lab report generally refers to, but it cannot diagnose or recommend treatment for you. Use it to prepare questions for your doctor, and see a medical professional for any personal health decision.
